name: The Malthusian Trap
statement: Population grows exponentially while food supply grows only linearly, so any gain in resources is eventually erased by population growth back to subsistence.
statementAccent: any gain in resources is eventually erased by population growth
meaning: The Malthusian trap holds that because population can grow geometrically while agricultural output grows only arithmetically, technological or resource gains temporarily raise living standards but soon trigger population growth that pushes per-capita resources back to a subsistence equilibrium. Pre-industrial societies are locked into a cycle where rising prosperity is checked by rising numbers. The trap breaks only when income growth outpaces population growth, as later occurred with industrialisation.
mechanism: Malthus argued two kinds of "checks" keep population near the resource ceiling: preventive checks (postponed marriage, celibacy) and positive checks (famine, disease, war that raise mortality). When resources temporarily expand, higher living standards encourage earlier marriage and more surviving children, so population rises until per-capita resources fall back to subsistence, restoring equilibrium.

examples.text: Economic historians describe most of human history before roughly 1800 as broadly Malthusian, where periodic famines, plagues such as the Black Death, and wars repeatedly reset population near subsistence despite episodes of technological improvement.

Economic historian Gregory Clark argues Britain’s 18th-19th century escape from the trap involved sustained productivity growth from industrialisation outrunning population growth for the first time, ending the cycle in developed economies.
Some contemporary economists argue parts of Sub-Saharan Africa still show Malthusian dynamics, where rapid population growth continues to strain agricultural capacity, though this claim is disputed.

whyItMatters: It remains a foundational reference in demography and development economics for understanding why sustained per-capita income growth is a recent, historically unusual phenomenon, and it frames debates about resource limits, population policy, and the demographic transition.
limits: The predicted catastrophe did not materialise in industrialised nations: mechanised agriculture, fertilisers, the Green Revolution, and the demographic transition (fertility falling with rising income) allowed sustained per-capita growth. Critics from Marx and Engels onward argued Malthus underestimated technological adaptability and wrongly blamed poverty on reproduction rather than institutions.
misreadings: It is commonly misread as a literal prediction that mass famine is imminent or inevitable everywhere; Malthus’s core logic describes a historical equilibrium dynamic that industrialised economies have empirically escaped, not an ironclad law of all times and places.
origin: Introduced by Thomas Robert Malthus in "An Essay on the Principle of Population," first published anonymously in 1798.

sources.text: Malthusianism, Wikipedia. — the mechanism of preventive and positive checks, origin, criticisms, and the industrial-revolution escape.
Malthus, "An Essay on the Principle of Population" (1798), Project Gutenberg. — the original argument that population grows geometrically against arithmetic growth in food.
